transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi… good to meet you too. I guess I came in because my worrying has gotten to the point where I can’t really put it away once it starts. Like, if I start worrying about my mother getting up at night, or a grant report I’m responsible for, or whether I missed some small thing at work, it just keeps going in my head.

I make lists—honestly, I make a lot of lists—and I try to tell myself, “Okay, you’ve handled what you can, move on,” but it doesn’t really work. It’s like I can’t shelve the worry in my mind, which is embarrassing to say as a librarian, but that’s exactly what it feels like. It just stays checked out, so to speak, and I keep circling back to it no matter how much I try to redirect myself.
Do these thoughts ever feel intrusive and unwanted, like they pop into your mind even when you don’t want them to?

Yes… I think that’s a good way to put it. They feel unwanted in the sense that I’ll be trying to do something completely ordinary, like focus on a report at work or just get through the evening, and then the worry sort of appears and takes over. It isn’t like I’m choosing to sit down and think through it carefully. Once it starts—whether it’s about my mother getting up at night, or whether I’ve missed some detail at work, or the grant report—it’s very hard to push it aside.

I’ll make lists, and then sometimes lists about the lists, trying to reassure myself that I’ve covered what I can. But even after that, my mind keeps circling back, like, “Are you sure? What if you forgot something?” So yes, they do feel intrusive, but mostly they feel… sticky, I guess. Like I can’t shelve them, no matter how much I tell myself to move on.
When these worries get stuck, do you find yourself doing anything over and over to feel less anxious, like checking, repeating, or going through something in your mind?

I’m not sure I’d call it repeating exactly… at least not in a ritual kind of way, if that’s what you mean. I don’t think I’m doing something like touching things a certain number of times or having to redo something in a very specific order.

What I do notice is that I’ll go back over things in my head a lot, and I do check lists or rewrite them because it makes me feel like I’m at least trying to get the worry under control. But I’m not sure where the line is between “being responsible” and “doing it over and over because I’m anxious.” With work things especially, I’ll think, “Let me just make sure I didn’t miss anything,” and then sometimes I’ve spent much longer than I meant to just reviewing the same thing mentally.

So… yes and no, I guess. I do circle back and reassure myself, but I don’t know if it’s a compulsion exactly. It feels more like I’m trying to calm myself down and be certain, and then I can’t quite get the certainty I’m looking for.
Do you find yourself worrying about many different parts of your life, rather than mainly one specific problem?

Yes, definitely. It used to feel more centered on my mother—like whether she was safe at night, whether I should be doing more, whether I’d missed some sign that she needed help. But over this past year it’s spread out, and now it feels like almost any category of my life can turn into something I worry about.

Finances, even if nothing immediate has happened. Staff decisions at work, like whether I handled a situation fairly or said the wrong thing. Deadlines, grant reports, house things I’ve been putting off, repairs, paperwork… and then this whole layer of, “Am I being a good daughter?” That one comes up a lot.

And the frustrating thing is that even small things don’t stay small in my mind. Something like an email I haven’t answered or a bill I need to double-check can start to feel like it’s the first loose thread and everything is about to unravel. I know that sounds dramatic when I say it out loud, but in the moment it really feels like if I don’t catch every detail, something will go wrong.
Do you feel that your worrying is more than the situation really calls for?

Yes… I think so. I mean, in the moment it feels completely justified, because my mind is telling me, “Well, if you don’t think this through, something bad could happen,” or “If you miss one detail, everything could unravel.” But when I step back, I can see that the level of worry is probably bigger than the actual situation.

Like, it started mostly with my mother’s safety, and that felt understandable to me. But now it’s not just that. It’s finances, staff decisions at work, deadlines, the house, things I need to fix or follow up on, whether I’m being a good daughter… it’s like almost anything can become the thing I latch onto. And the size of the worry doesn’t always match the size of the problem. An unanswered email or a bill I need to double-check can start to feel like some huge warning sign, like if I don’t handle it perfectly, then everything is going to fall apart.

So yes, I do think it’s more than the situation calls for. I don’t always believe that when I’m in it, but afterward I can usually see that my reaction was bigger than what was actually happening.
When these thoughts come up, do they feel like they don’t make sense or are excessive, even while you’re having them?

Yes… I think part of me knows they’re excessive, even while it’s happening, but it doesn’t really stop them. It’s like I can hear a quieter, more reasonable voice saying, “This is probably bigger than it needs to be,” but the anxious part is much louder and says, “No, you have to keep thinking about it because something could go wrong.”

And it’s not just one topic anymore. Over this past year, it’s gone from mostly being about my mother’s safety to… finances, decisions I’ve made with staff, deadlines, things with the house, and then this constant question of whether I’m being a good daughter. So when a small thing comes up, like something I haven’t finished or something I need to double-check, it can suddenly feel like everything is about to unravel if I don’t get on top of it immediately.

So yes, even in the moment I sometimes know it’s too much, or at least that it doesn’t fully make sense. But it still feels urgent. That’s the hard part.
Have you generally seen your need for order, lists, and getting things exactly right as just part of your personality, even when you weren’t especially anxious?

I’m not sure, honestly. I can see that I’ve always liked things to be organized, especially with work—lists, systems, knowing where things are—but I don’t know if I’d say I’ve always needed things to be exactly right in a rigid way.

I mean, being a librarian, there’s a certain amount of order that just feels natural, or even necessary. I’m used to tracking details and making lists and having categories for things, so it’s hard for me to separate what’s just my work style or personality from what might be something more. I’ve probably always been someone who feels better when there’s a plan, but I don’t know that I noticed it as a problem when I wasn’t anxious.

So… I guess my answer is maybe, but I’m not completely sure what counts. It didn’t stand out to me as something extreme before, if that makes sense.
Did this increase in worrying begin after a specific stressful event or change in your life?

Yes. It really seemed to start after my mother fell and then moved into my home. That was… about a year and two months ago now, I think. It’s strange because at first I saw it as just a normal reaction—she’d had this scary fall, and suddenly my house and my routines and my responsibilities all changed at once.

Before that, I worried about things, of course, but not like this. After she came to live with me, it felt like there was always something I needed to anticipate or prevent. I kept thinking, “What if she falls again?” or “What if I miss something?” And then over time the worry sort of spread out from there. But if I had to point to when it really increased, yes, it was when she moved in after the fall, about fourteen months ago.
Has this level of worrying been present most days for at least six months?

Yes… definitely most days, and for longer than six months. It’s been about a year and two months now, really since my mother moved into my home after her fall.

At first I kept thinking it was just temporary, like I was adjusting to a big change, but it hasn’t really let up in the way I expected. So yes, if you’re asking whether this level of worry has been there most days for at least six months, I’d say yes—more like fourteen months.
When you go back over lists or review things in your mind, does it feel like you have to do it to relieve the anxiety, even when you know it’s excessive?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that. I do go back over lists and things in my head, yes, but I don’t know if it feels like a “have to” in the way you mean.

Sometimes it’s more like… if I don’t review it, I feel unsettled, like I might be missing something important. So I’ll look again, or mentally walk through what needs to happen, and it can make me feel a little calmer for the moment. But I’m not always aware of it as, “I’m doing this to relieve anxiety.” It just feels practical at the time, like I’m trying to be responsible or make sure nothing slips through.

I can also tell that sometimes it’s probably more than necessary, especially when I’ve already checked and I’m still thinking about it. But I don’t know that I’d describe it as a ritual exactly. It’s more this nagging sense that reviewing things will help me feel more prepared, even if part of me knows I may be overdoing it.
If you try not to go back over a list or mentally review something, do you feel that something bad might happen because you didn’t check?

Yes… I think that’s exactly what it feels like, even if I don’t always say it to myself that directly. It’s not usually some very specific belief like, “If I don’t check this list, then this exact terrible thing will happen,” but it’s more this awful feeling that if I don’t go back over it, I’ll have missed something important and then something will go wrong.

Like with my mother, if I don’t mentally review whether she has what she needs, or whether I heard her get up, or whether something is in the right place, I start imagining that maybe she’ll get up at night and I won’t notice, or I’ll have failed to anticipate something. And at work it’s similar—if I don’t go back over a grant report or some detail in a project, I get stuck on the idea that I may have overlooked something and it’ll create a problem later.

The frustrating thing is, even when I do make lists or check things, the worry doesn’t really stay put. Once it starts, I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind, which is ironic given my job. I can try to redirect myself, or tell myself I already checked, but it keeps coming back around. So yes, I guess I do feel like not reviewing means I’m leaving the door open for something bad to happen, even if I also know I may be overdoing it.
Do you ever feel that checking or mentally reviewing something prevents a bad outcome, even when you know logically it probably doesn’t?

Yes… I think I do feel that way, at least emotionally. Logically, I know making another list or mentally walking through something for the third or fourth time doesn’t actually control what happens. It doesn’t guarantee my mother won’t get up at night, or that I didn’t miss some detail in a grant report, or that everything at work will go smoothly.

But once the worry starts, it’s like I can’t shelve it in my mind. That’s honestly part of why I came in. I’ll try to redirect myself, or tell myself, “You already checked this,” or “You’ve made the list,” but it keeps circling back. And in the moment, reviewing it feels like the only thing I can do to prevent something from slipping through. Even if I know, rationally, that it probably isn’t preventing a bad outcome in any real way, it still feels safer than not doing it.
Do these thoughts ever take the form of disturbing images or impulses, rather than just worries about real-life problems?

I don’t think so… at least not in the way I imagine you mean. It’s usually not like a sudden disturbing picture or an urge to do something. It’s more verbal, more like a loop of “what if I forgot this” or “what if something goes wrong because I didn’t think it through.”

I do sometimes picture possible outcomes in a general way, like imagining something going wrong if I’ve missed a detail, but I wouldn’t call them intrusive images exactly. They’re not bizarre or out of nowhere. They’re tied to whatever I’m already worried about, and they feel like my mind trying to anticipate problems, even if it goes too far.

And I don’t really have impulses, no. It’s more that I feel pulled to think through things or check them again, not that I’m afraid I’ll do some disturbing thing. So… I guess I’d say it’s mostly worries about real-life problems, just repeated and hard to put down.
If your mother were no longer living with you, do you think this level of worrying would still be there?

Yes… I think it would. I mean, my mother living with me is a big part of it, and I don’t want to minimize that because her safety is probably the thing that started taking up the most space in my head. But over this past year, it hasn’t stayed neatly in that one area.

It’s like the worrying has spread into everything. I worry about money and whether I’m planning well enough. I worry about staff decisions at work, whether I handled something fairly or missed some implication. Deadlines can start to feel much bigger than they are, like if I don’t stay on top of every piece, the whole thing will unravel. Even things around the house—small repairs, bills, whether I remembered to do something—can suddenly feel urgent or consequential.

And then there’s this whole other layer of whether I’m being a good daughter, which I suppose would still be there even if she weren’t living with me. Maybe it would look different, but I don’t think it would just disappear. I wish I could say, “Oh, if that one situation changed, I’d feel normal again,” but honestly I think my mind would find other things to latch onto. It already has.
When you check or mentally review things, does it feel like you must do it until it feels just right or complete?

I’m not sure it’s exactly a “just right” feeling, if that makes sense. It’s not like I’m trying to get a sensation of completeness in a particular way, or that I have to repeat something until it lands perfectly.

It’s more that I don’t feel reassured yet, so I go back over it again. Like, if I’m reviewing an email or a work detail, I’m not thinking, “This has to feel just right.” I’m thinking, “What if I missed something?” And then I check again because I still feel uneasy. Sometimes there is a point where I think, okay, I’ve done enough, but it’s not a very satisfying or clean feeling. It’s more like I’m tired or I’ve run out of time, or I’m telling myself I have to stop.

So… I don’t know. “Complete” maybe a little, but not in a ritual sort of way. More like I’m trying to quiet the uncertainty, and the checking is an attempt to get to a place where I can move on. But it doesn’t always work.
On a typical day, how much time do you spend checking things or reviewing them in your mind?

It varies, but… more than I want to admit, probably. It’s not always one obvious block of time where I’m sitting there checking a door or rereading something for an hour. It’s more scattered through the day, which almost makes it harder to measure.

If I’m at work and something sets it off—like a grant report, or an email, or whether I missed some detail in a collection request—I can lose chunks of time going back over it. Ten minutes here, twenty minutes there, sometimes longer if I’m really stuck. And then even after I’ve technically moved on, I’ll still be reviewing it in my head while I’m trying to do something else.

At home it’s similar with my mother. If I’m worried about her getting up at night, I might check things, make a list, remind myself what’s already handled… but the worry doesn’t really stay put. Once it starts, I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind. That’s actually a good way to put it, because I keep wanting to put it away and move on to the next thing, and it just keeps sliding back out.

So on a typical day… maybe altogether it’s easily an hour or two, sometimes more, if you count the mental reviewing and not just the physical checking. The frustrating part is that making lists or trying to redirect myself doesn’t reliably stop it. It helps me function, but it doesn’t necessarily quiet my mind.
Do you experience the checking and mental reviewing as something unreasonable that you feel driven to do, rather than simply as worrying a lot?

I think it’s closer to feeling driven to do it, but I don’t always experience it as “unreasonable” in the moment. That’s part of what makes it confusing. When I’m in it, it feels like I’m being responsible, like if I just review the grant report one more time, or think through whether I missed something at work, or make another list about my mother getting up at night, then maybe I can prevent something from going wrong.

But stepping back, yes, I can see that it goes beyond ordinary worrying. I came in because once a worry starts, I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind. It keeps demanding attention even after I’ve done the sensible things—made the list, checked the detail, reminded myself that I already handled it. I’ll try to redirect myself, and it’s like my mind just circles back anyway.

So I don’t know that I’d call it a ritual exactly, but it does feel like I’m pulled into it. I don’t feel free to just say, “That’s enough,” and move on. I want to, but I often can’t.
When you start mentally reviewing something, does it feel like you’re doing it to neutralize the anxiety?

Yes… I think so, though I don’t know if I would have used the word “neutralize” before. It’s more like I’m trying to calm the alarm in my head, or make the worry settle down enough that I can put it away.

Like, if it’s about my mother getting up at night, I’ll start reviewing what I’ve done, what I need to remember, whether I made a list, whether there’s something I’m forgetting. Or with a grant report or something at work, I’ll replay the details and think, “Did I miss something? Did I overlook a problem?” And I think the purpose of doing that is to reassure myself, yes—to make the anxiety quiet down.

The problem is it doesn’t really stay quiet. That’s why I came in, honestly. Once a worry starts, I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind, no matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself. I can tell myself, “You’ve already thought this through,” but then a few minutes later it’s back, and I’m reviewing it again. So yes, I think I’m trying to reduce the anxiety, but it doesn’t work very well, or not for long.
When the urge to mentally review or check comes up, do you try to resist doing it?

I do try to resist it, yes… at least I think I do. I’ll tell myself, “No, you already checked that,” or “You already made the list,” or “You’re not going to solve anything by going over this again.” And sometimes I really make an effort to redirect myself—move on to another task, answer a different email, get up and do something practical.

But the problem is that once the worry starts, it feels like it has its own momentum. If it’s about my mother getting up at night, or a grant report, or whether I missed something at work, I can try very hard to put it aside, but it doesn’t stay aside. It’s like I’m trying to shelve it in my mind, and it keeps sliding back out again. I know that sounds a little silly, but that’s honestly how it feels.

Lists help a little in the sense that they give me something concrete to point to, like, “See, you handled this.” But they don’t reliably stop the urge to review. I can make the list, check the detail, remind myself I’ve done what I can, and then five or ten minutes later my mind is back at it again. So yes, I resist it, but I don’t feel very successful at resisting it.
Do these thoughts feel like your own normal worries, or do they feel alien or senseless to you?

They feel like my own worries, not alien exactly. I mean, they’re about real things in my life—my mother getting up at night, a grant report, whether I missed something at work—so they don’t feel senseless in the way of coming out of nowhere.

But they do feel… excessive, I guess, or hard to get out from under. That’s really why I came in. Once one of those worries starts, I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind. Even if I make lists, even if I check what I need to check, even if I try to redirect myself and say, “Okay, you’ve done what you can,” it doesn’t stay put away. It keeps coming back up.

So no, I wouldn’t say they feel foreign to me. They feel like my normal worries, just turned up too high and kind of stuck on repeat.

I mean, in the moment it feels completely justified, because my mind is telling me, “Well, if you don’t think this through, something bad could happen,” or “If you miss one detail, everything could unravel.” But when I step back, I can see that the level of worry is probably bigger than the actual situation.

Like, it started mostly with my mother’s safety, and that felt understandable to me. But now it’s not just that. It’s finances, staff decisions at work, deadlines, the house, things I need to fix or follow up on, whether I’m being a good daughter… it’s like almost anything can become the thing I latch onto. And the size of the worry doesn’t always match the size of the problem. An unanswered email or a bill I need to double-check can start to feel like some huge warning sign, like if I don’t handle it perfectly, then everything is going to fall apart.

So yes, I do think it’s more than the situation calls for. I don’t always believe that when I’m in it, but afterward I can usually see that my reaction was bigger than what was actually happening.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences true obsessions as irrational, ego-dystonic thoughts, which would help distinguish OCD from generalized anxiety or obsessive-compulsive personality traits.
doctor.question: When these thoughts come up, do they feel like they don’t make sense or are excessive, even while you’re having them?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: Over this past year my worrying has spread from just my mother’s safety to finances, staff decisions, deadlines, the house, and whether I’m being a good daughter, and even small things can start to feel like they’re about to unravel.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the worries feel excessive or unreasonable while they are happening, which directly relates to excessive anxiety and worry.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think part of me knows they’re excessive, even while it’s happening, but it doesn’t really stop them. It’s like I can hear a quieter, more reasonable voice saying, “This is probably bigger than it needs to be,” but the anxious part is much louder and says, “No, you have to keep thinking about it because something could go wrong.”

And it’s not just one topic anymore. Over this past year, it’s gone from mostly being about my mother’s safety to… finances, decisions I’ve made with staff, deadlines, things with the house, and then this constant question of whether I’m being a good daughter. So when a small thing comes up, like something I haven’t finished or something I need to double-check, it can suddenly feel like everything is about to unravel if I don’t get on top of it immediately.

So yes, even in the moment I sometimes know it’s too much, or at least that it doesn’t fully make sense. But it still feels urgent. That’s the hard part.

doctor.intent: Differentiate ego-syntonic perfectionism/control traits of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder from ego-dystonic anxiety/obsessional symptoms.
doctor.question: Have you generally seen your need for order, lists, and getting things exactly right as just part of your personality, even when you weren’t especially anxious?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about longstanding personality traits related to order, lists, and perfectionism outside of anxiety, which is not covered by the provided GAD symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure, honestly. I can see that I’ve always liked things to be organized, especially with work—lists, systems, knowing where things are—but I don’t know if I’d say I’ve always needed things to be exactly right in a rigid way.

I mean, being a librarian, there’s a certain amount of order that just feels natural, or even necessary. I’m used to tracking details and making lists and having categories for things, so it’s hard for me to separate what’s just my work style or personality from what might be something more. I’ve probably always been someone who feels better when there’s a plan, but I don’t know that I noticed it as a problem when I wasn’t anxious.

So… I guess my answer is maybe, but I’m not completely sure what counts. It didn’t stand out to me as something extreme before, if that makes sense.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms are tied to an identifiable recent stressor, which would help distinguish adjustment disorder from generalized anxiety disorder or OCD-spectrum conditions.
doctor.question: Did this increase in worrying begin after a specific stressful event or change in your life?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about a year and two months, since my mother moved into my home after her fall.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about when the increased worrying began and whether it followed a specific life change; the duration profile notes it has been going on for about a year and two months since the patient's mother moved in after her fall.

patient.answer:
Yes. It really seemed to start after my mother fell and then moved into my home. That was… about a year and two months ago now, I think. It’s strange because at first I saw it as just a normal reaction—she’d had this scary fall, and suddenly my house and my routines and my responsibilities all changed at once.

Before that, I worried about things, of course, but not like this. After she came to live with me, it felt like there was always something I needed to anticipate or prevent. I kept thinking, “What if she falls again?” or “What if I miss something?” And then over time the worry sort of spread out from there. But if I had to point to when it really increased, yes, it was when she moved in after the fall, about fourteen months ago.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the anxiety has been present for at least 6 months, which helps distinguish generalized anxiety disorder from adjustment disorder with anxiety.
doctor.question: Has this level of worrying been present most days for at least six months?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about a year and two months, since my mother moved into my home after her fall.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the worrying has been present, specifically whether it has lasted most days for at least six months.

patient.answer:
Yes… definitely most days, and for longer than six months. It’s been about a year and two months now, really since my mother moved into my home after her fall.

At first I kept thinking it was just temporary, like I was adjusting to a big change, but it hasn’t really let up in the way I expected. So yes, if you’re asking whether this level of worry has been there most days for at least six months, I’d say yes—more like fourteen months.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the repetitive reviewing and list-checking is a true compulsion performed to neutralize anxiety, which would help distinguish OCD from generalized anxiety and personality-based orderliness.
doctor.question: When you go back over lists or review things in your mind, does it feel like you have to do it to relieve the anxiety, even when you know it’s excessive?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about compulsive reviewing/checking done to relieve anxiety despite knowing it is excessive, which is more specific than the provided GAD symptom profiles and is not directly covered by any listed item.

patient.answer:
I’m not completely sure how to answer that. I do go back over lists and things in my head, yes, but I don’t know if it feels like a “have to” in the way you mean.

Sometimes it’s more like… if I don’t review it, I feel unsettled, like I might be missing something important. So I’ll look again, or mentally walk through what needs to happen, and it can make me feel a little calmer for the moment. But I’m not always aware of it as, “I’m doing this to relieve anxiety.” It just feels practical at the time, like I’m trying to be responsible or make sure nothing slips through.

I can also tell that sometimes it’s probably more than necessary, especially when I’ve already checked and I’m still thinking about it. But I don’t know that I’d describe it as a ritual exactly. It’s more this nagging sense that reviewing things will help me feel more prepared, even if part of me knows I may be overdoing it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the repetitive reviewing/list-checking is driven by a feared consequence if it is not done, which would help distinguish OCD from generalized anxiety and personality-based perfectionism.
doctor.question: If you try not to go back over a list or mentally review something, do you feel that something bad might happen because you didn’t check?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I came in because once a worry starts—about my mother getting up at night, a grant report, or whether I missed something at work—I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind, no matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself.
target_item.reason: The question is about whether not checking or mentally reviewing leaves me unable to settle the worry and feeling that something may go wrong if I don’t keep reviewing it.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think that’s exactly what it feels like, even if I don’t always say it to myself that directly. It’s not usually some very specific belief like, “If I don’t check this list, then this exact terrible thing will happen,” but it’s more this awful feeling that if I don’t go back over it, I’ll have missed something important and then something will go wrong.

Like with my mother, if I don’t mentally review whether she has what she needs, or whether I heard her get up, or whether something is in the right place, I start imagining that maybe she’ll get up at night and I won’t notice, or I’ll have failed to anticipate something. And at work it’s similar—if I don’t go back over a grant report or some detail in a project, I get stuck on the idea that I may have overlooked something and it’ll create a problem later.

The frustrating thing is, even when I do make lists or check things, the worry doesn’t really stay put. Once it starts, I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind, which is ironic given my job. I can try to redirect myself, or tell myself I already checked, but it keeps coming back around. So yes, I guess I do feel like not reviewing means I’m leaving the door open for something bad to happen, even if I also know I may be overdoing it.

doctor.intent: Differentiate ego-dystonic obsessions/compulsions in OCD from more realistic generalized worry by testing for irrational magical or catastrophe-prevention beliefs tied to checking/reviewing.
doctor.question: Do you ever feel that checking or mentally reviewing something prevents a bad outcome, even when you know logically it probably doesn’t?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I came in because once a worry starts—about my mother getting up at night, a grant report, or whether I missed something at work—I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind, no matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself.
target_item.reason: The question is most directly about the mental reviewing/checking that comes from worry and the difficulty letting the worry stop even when logically it may be excessive.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think I do feel that way, at least emotionally. Logically, I know making another list or mentally walking through something for the third or fourth time doesn’t actually control what happens. It doesn’t guarantee my mother won’t get up at night, or that I didn’t miss some detail in a grant report, or that everything at work will go smoothly.

But once the worry starts, it’s like I can’t shelve it in my mind. That’s honestly part of why I came in. I’ll try to redirect myself, or tell myself, “You already checked this,” or “You’ve made the list,” but it keeps circling back. And in the moment, reviewing it feels like the only thing I can do to prevent something from slipping through. Even if I know, rationally, that it probably isn’t preventing a bad outcome in any real way, it still feels safer than not doing it.

inference.note: Removed F60.5 because the need for order/lists does not appear to be a longstanding ego-syntonic personality pattern; current turn strengthens OCD-spectrum features via anxiety-relieving checking/mental reviewing with feared bad outcomes, while GAD remains likely given excessive multi-domain worry >6 months and onset after stressor also keeps adjustment disorder on the differential.

doctor.intent: Differentiate generalized anxiety disorder from obsessive-compulsive disorder by determining whether the recurrent thoughts are experienced as obsessional impulses/images rather than ordinary worries about real-life problems.
doctor.question: Do these thoughts ever take the form of disturbing images or impulses, rather than just worries about real-life problems?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about disturbing intrusive images or impulses, which is not covered by the provided symptom profiles; the profiles describe generalized real-life worries rather than obsessional images or impulses.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… at least not in the way I imagine you mean. It’s usually not like a sudden disturbing picture or an urge to do something. It’s more verbal, more like a loop of “what if I forgot this” or “what if something goes wrong because I didn’t think it through.”

I do sometimes picture possible outcomes in a general way, like imagining something going wrong if I’ve missed a detail, but I wouldn’t call them intrusive images exactly. They’re not bizarre or out of nowhere. They’re tied to whatever I’m already worried about, and they feel like my mind trying to anticipate problems, even if it goes too far.

And I don’t really have impulses, no. It’s more that I feel pulled to think through things or check them again, not that I’m afraid I’ll do some disturbing thing. So… I guess I’d say it’s mostly worries about real-life problems, just repeated and hard to put down.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the worry is confined to the stressor involving her mother or has clearly generalized beyond it, to distinguish adjustment disorder with anxiety from generalized anxiety disorder.
doctor.question: If your mother were no longer living with you, do you think this level of worrying would still be there?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: Over this past year my worrying has spread from just my mother’s safety to finances, staff decisions, deadlines, the house, and whether I’m being a good daughter, and even small things can start to feel like they’re about to unravel.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the worrying is generalized and would persist beyond the specific stressor of the mother living with the patient, which matches excessive anxiety and worry across multiple events or activities.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think it would. I mean, my mother living with me is a big part of it, and I don’t want to minimize that because her safety is probably the thing that started taking up the most space in my head. But over this past year, it hasn’t stayed neatly in that one area.

It’s like the worrying has spread into everything. I worry about money and whether I’m planning well enough. I worry about staff decisions at work, whether I handled something fairly or missed some implication. Deadlines can start to feel much bigger than they are, like if I don’t stay on top of every piece, the whole thing will unravel. Even things around the house—small repairs, bills, whether I remembered to do something—can suddenly feel urgent or consequential.

And then there’s this whole other layer of whether I’m being a good daughter, which I suppose would still be there even if she weren’t living with me. Maybe it would look different, but I don’t think it would just disappear. I wish I could say, “Oh, if that one situation changed, I’d feel normal again,” but honestly I think my mind would find other things to latch onto. It already has.

doctor.intent: Differentiate generalized anxiety disorder from obsessive-compulsive disorder by clarifying whether the repeated checking/reviewing is a true compulsion driven by rigid internal rules rather than ordinary worry-driven reassurance.
doctor.question: When you check or mentally review things, does it feel like you must do it until it feels just right or complete?

target_item.reason: The question asks about a compulsive 'just right' or completeness feeling when checking or mentally reviewing, which is not covered by the provided GAD symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure it’s exactly a “just right” feeling, if that makes sense. It’s not like I’m trying to get a sensation of completeness in a particular way, or that I have to repeat something until it lands perfectly.

It’s more that I don’t feel reassured yet, so I go back over it again. Like, if I’m reviewing an email or a work detail, I’m not thinking, “This has to feel just right.” I’m thinking, “What if I missed something?” And then I check again because I still feel uneasy. Sometimes there is a point where I think, okay, I’ve done enough, but it’s not a very satisfying or clean feeling. It’s more like I’m tired or I’ve run out of time, or I’m telling myself I have to stop.

So… I don’t know. “Complete” maybe a little, but not in a ritual sort of way. More like I’m trying to quiet the uncertainty, and the checking is an attempt to get to a place where I can move on. But it doesn’t always work.

doctor.intent: Differentiate OCD from generalized anxiety or adjustment disorder by determining whether the checking/mental reviewing is excessively time-consuming.
doctor.question: On a typical day, how much time do you spend checking things or reviewing them in your mind?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I came in because once a worry starts—about my mother getting up at night, a grant report, or whether I missed something at work—I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind, no matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about time spent checking or mentally reviewing, which in this profile is best understood as part of being unable to stop or control worry once it starts.

patient.answer:
It varies, but… more than I want to admit, probably. It’s not always one obvious block of time where I’m sitting there checking a door or rereading something for an hour. It’s more scattered through the day, which almost makes it harder to measure.

If I’m at work and something sets it off—like a grant report, or an email, or whether I missed some detail in a collection request—I can lose chunks of time going back over it. Ten minutes here, twenty minutes there, sometimes longer if I’m really stuck. And then even after I’ve technically moved on, I’ll still be reviewing it in my head while I’m trying to do something else.

At home it’s similar with my mother. If I’m worried about her getting up at night, I might check things, make a list, remind myself what’s already handled… but the worry doesn’t really stay put. Once it starts, I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind. That’s actually a good way to put it, because I keep wanting to put it away and move on to the next thing, and it just keeps sliding back out.

So on a typical day… maybe altogether it’s easily an hour or two, sometimes more, if you count the mental reviewing and not just the physical checking. The frustrating part is that making lists or trying to redirect myself doesn’t reliably stop it. It helps me function, but it doesn’t necessarily quiet my mind.

inference.note: Ruled out F43.22 because symptoms have persisted >6 months and generalized across multiple domains beyond the original stressor. Current turn supports possible compulsive checking/mental reviewing taking 1–2+ hours/day, but obsessions are mainly real-life worries rather than classic OCD intrusions, so keep F41.1 and F42.9.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the repeated checking and mental reviewing are ego-dystonic compulsions driven by obsessions, which would favor OCD over generalized anxiety disorder.
doctor.question: Do you experience the checking and mental reviewing as something unreasonable that you feel driven to do, rather than simply as worrying a lot?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I came in because once a worry starts—about my mother getting up at night, a grant report, or whether I missed something at work—I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind, no matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the checking and mental reviewing are better understood as compulsive acts or as worry that is hard to control; the relevant profile item is the difficulty stopping or controlling worry.

patient.answer:
I think it’s closer to feeling driven to do it, but I don’t always experience it as “unreasonable” in the moment. That’s part of what makes it confusing. When I’m in it, it feels like I’m being responsible, like if I just review the grant report one more time, or think through whether I missed something at work, or make another list about my mother getting up at night, then maybe I can prevent something from going wrong.

But stepping back, yes, I can see that it goes beyond ordinary worrying. I came in because once a worry starts, I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind. It keeps demanding attention even after I’ve done the sensible things—made the list, checked the detail, reminded myself that I already handled it. I’ll try to redirect myself, and it’s like my mind just circles back anyway.

So I don’t know that I’d call it a ritual exactly, but it does feel like I’m pulled into it. I don’t feel free to just say, “That’s enough,” and move on. I want to, but I often can’t.

doctor.intent: Differentiate generalized anxiety disorder from OCD by determining whether the repetitive mental reviewing is specifically aimed at neutralizing anxiety from intrusive thoughts, i.e., a true compulsion.
doctor.question: When you start mentally reviewing something, does it feel like you’re doing it to neutralize the anxiety?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I came in because once a worry starts—about my mother getting up at night, a grant report, or whether I missed something at work—I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind, no matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself.
target_item.reason: The question is about mental reviewing as a response to anxiety, and the closest profile item is the difficulty stopping or controlling worry once it starts.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think so, though I don’t know if I would have used the word “neutralize” before. It’s more like I’m trying to calm the alarm in my head, or make the worry settle down enough that I can put it away.

Like, if it’s about my mother getting up at night, I’ll start reviewing what I’ve done, what I need to remember, whether I made a list, whether there’s something I’m forgetting. Or with a grant report or something at work, I’ll replay the details and think, “Did I miss something? Did I overlook a problem?” And I think the purpose of doing that is to reassure myself, yes—to make the anxiety quiet down.

The problem is it doesn’t really stay quiet. That’s why I came in, honestly. Once a worry starts, I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind, no matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself. I can tell myself, “You’ve already thought this through,” but then a few minutes later it’s back, and I’m reviewing it again. So yes, I think I’m trying to reduce the anxiety, but it doesn’t work very well, or not for long.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the repeated mental reviewing/checking is ego-dystonic and resisted like a compulsion, which best distinguishes OCD from generalized worry.
doctor.question: When the urge to mentally review or check comes up, do you try to resist doing it?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I came in because once a worry starts—about my mother getting up at night, a grant report, or whether I missed something at work—I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind, no matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself.
target_item.reason: The question is about whether she can resist or control the urge to mentally review/check when worry comes up, which most directly matches difficulty stopping or controlling worry.

patient.answer:
I do try to resist it, yes… at least I think I do. I’ll tell myself, “No, you already checked that,” or “You already made the list,” or “You’re not going to solve anything by going over this again.” And sometimes I really make an effort to redirect myself—move on to another task, answer a different email, get up and do something practical.

But the problem is that once the worry starts, it feels like it has its own momentum. If it’s about my mother getting up at night, or a grant report, or whether I missed something at work, I can try very hard to put it aside, but it doesn’t stay aside. It’s like I’m trying to shelve it in my mind, and it keeps sliding back out again. I know that sounds a little silly, but that’s honestly how it feels.

Lists help a little in the sense that they give me something concrete to point to, like, “See, you handled this.” But they don’t reliably stop the urge to review. I can make the list, check the detail, remind myself I’ve done what I can, and then five or ten minutes later my mind is back at it again. So yes, I resist it, but I don’t feel very successful at resisting it.

doctor.intent: Differentiate obsessional mental checking from generalized worry by assessing whether the thoughts are ego-dystonic and feel separate from ordinary concerns.
doctor.question: Do these thoughts feel like your own normal worries, or do they feel alien or senseless to you?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I came in because once a worry starts—about my mother getting up at night, a grant report, or whether I missed something at work—I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind, no matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself.
target_item.reason: The question is about how the recurrent thoughts are experienced, and the closest matching profile is the patient’s uncontrollable worry—ordinary worries that become difficult to stop or set aside, rather than alien or senseless thoughts.

patient.answer:
They feel like my own worries, not alien exactly. I mean, they’re about real things in my life—my mother getting up at night, a grant report, whether I missed something at work—so they don’t feel senseless in the way of coming out of nowhere.

But they do feel… excessive, I guess, or hard to get out from under. That’s really why I came in. Once one of those worries starts, I can’t seem to shelve it in my mind. Even if I make lists, even if I check what I need to check, even if I try to redirect myself and say, “Okay, you’ve done what you can,” it doesn’t stay put away. It keeps coming back up.

So no, I wouldn’t say they feel foreign to me. They feel like my normal worries, just turned up too high and kind of stuck on repeat.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient’s main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes excessive, hard-to-control worry about multiple real-life domains occurring most days for about 14 months, with insight that the worry is disproportionate and not limited to a single obsessional theme. Although there is repetitive checking and mental review, these behaviors appear secondary to generalized worry about everyday problems rather than clear ego-dystonic obsessions with distinct compulsions or ritualized phenomena typical of OCD.
